key_terms.meaning: Application-Specific Integrated Circuit: a chip built for one fixed function, not reprogrammable after manufacture
Register-Transfer Level: a description of a circuit as registers plus the combinational logic and clocked transfers between them
The back-end stage that turns a gate netlist into layout: floorplan, placement, routing and signoff checks
Design for Testability: extra on-chip hardware such as scan chains added so a tester can control and observe internal nodes
Automatic Test Pattern Generation: CAD software that derives input patterns which excite a fault and push its effect to an output
Built-In Self-Test: on-chip pattern generator plus response checker that tests a block without an external tester
The final gate before tapeout where timing, power, noise, DRC and LVS reports must all pass their limits
A design style that uses pre-built cells or array fabric (standard cells, gate arrays) and customises only the wiring
The basic Verilog design block: a named unit with a port list and a body containing instances, assignments or always blocks
Describing a circuit by continuous assignments that show the flow of data from inputs to outputs, e.g. assign y = a & b;
Describing what a circuit does with algorithms inside always/initial blocks, without naming gates or wires
A Verilog module with no ports that applies stimulus to a design and checks its responses during simulation
Design Under Test: the module instance that a test bench drives and observes
Lookup Table: a small memory in an FPGA that stores the truth table of a logic function, so any k-input function fits in one cell
Field-Programmable Gate Array: a chip of configurable logic cells, routing and I/O blocks that the user programs after manufacture
Deciding where each major block, macro and I/O pin sits on the die before detailed placement
Fixing the exact die position of every standard cell so that wiring length and congestion stay low
Drawing the actual metal wires and vias that connect placed cells, in global and then detailed steps
A synthesizable HDL description of a block, delivered as source and mapped to any technology by the user
A processor delivered as synthesizable HDL and built from the FPGA or ASIC fabric itself, so its logic cost is paid in cells

takeaways: A VLSI flow runs specification, architecture, RTL, verification, synthesis, DFT insertion, physical design and signoff, and each stage hands a checked artifact to the next.
Test is a design task, not a final chore: DFT hardware is inserted at RTL or synthesis time, and ATPG patterns are generated once the netlist is stable.
A Verilog module with its port list is the unit of design and of reuse; nets carry values driven by continuous assignments, variables hold values assigned in procedural blocks.
Gate-level, dataflow and behavioural styles describe the same circuit at different abstraction, and only the synthesizable subset of behavioural code becomes hardware.
A test bench drives the DUT, waits with #delays or clock edges, and compares outputs, so errors are caught in simulation instead of in silicon.
An FPGA gives an array of LUTs, flip-flops, routing and I/O blocks that a bitstream configures, trading speed and area for zero mask cost.
Floorplanning, placement and routing decide wire length, congestion, timing and power; a bad floorplan cannot be repaired by a good router.
IP cores (soft, firm or hard) and soft-core processors let a system-on-chip reuse verified blocks, with wrappers handling bus protocols and clock-domain crossing.
bank_note: Long answers here are usually built around the design flow diagram with its artifacts, the three Verilog modelling styles shown with short code, and FPGA architecture — so draw the figure first, then label each stage with its input, output and check.

bank.q: Draw the VLSI design flow from specification to signoff. Explain each stage and state the artifact it produces.
outline: Specification and architecture: function, performance, power budget, block partition
RTL coding of each block with a test bench; functional verification against the spec
Synthesis to a gate netlist mapped to a standard-cell library
DFT insertion (scan chains, BIST) and ATPG pattern generation
Floorplan, placement, clock-tree synthesis, routing
Signoff: static timing, power, DRC/LVS, then tapeout
State the artifact of each stage: spec, RTL, netlist, placed-and-routed layout, test patterns, GDSII

bank.q: Classify Verilog operators into arithmetic, bitwise, reduction, logical, relational, shift, conditional and concatenation, and give a one-line example of each.
outline: Arithmetic: +, -, *, /, % on vectors, sized results
Bitwise: &, |, ^, ~ operate bit by bit on equal-width operands
Reduction: unary &, |, ^ fold all bits of one operand into a single bit
Logical: &&, ||, ! treat a nonzero vector as true and return 1 bit
Relational and equality: <, >, <=, >=, ==, != return 1 bit
Shift: <<, >> shift bits and leave zero fill
Conditional: cond ? a : b is a two-way select
Concatenation and replication: {a,b} and {n{a}}

bank.q: Compare gate-level, dataflow and behavioural modelling. Show the same 2-to-1 multiplexer in all three styles.
outline: Gate level: primitive instances (and, or, not) or instantiated cells; closest to the netlist
Dataflow: continuous assign with operators; shows data movement
Behavioural: always block with if/else or case; algorithmic, needs synthesis rules
Code for each style of the same mux
Which style is used for structural netlists, which for arithmetic, which for control logic and FSMs

bank.q: Describe the architecture of an FPGA: logic cells, LUTs, flip-flops, routing and I/O blocks. How is the function configured?
outline: Array of configurable logic blocks (CLBs); each CLB holds LUTs, flip-flops and carry logic
A k-input LUT is a 2^k x 1 memory that stores the truth table, so any k-input function fits
Programmable interconnect: switch boxes and connection boxes driven by configuration bits
I/O blocks with selectable standards and registers
Configuration memory loaded as a bitstream at power-up
Trade-off versus ASIC: no mask cost, lower speed and higher area

bank.q: What is design for testability? Explain scan insertion, ATPG and BIST, and where the DUT and tester fit in the flow.
outline: Why testing matters: stuck-at and other faults, defective parts must be screened
Scan: flip-flops replaced by scan flip-flops chained into shift registers, giving controllability and observability
ATPG: excite a fault, propagate to an output, generate compact pattern sets
BIST: on-chip LFSR pattern generator plus signature analyser (MISR)
Flow position: DFT insertion after synthesis, patterns after netlist, DUT tested on ATE with test program
Metrics: fault coverage, pattern count, test time and test cost

bank.q: Write a synthesizable Verilog module for a 4-bit synchronous up counter with asynchronous reset. Add a test bench, and explain how it is compiled and simulated.
outline: Module declaration with ports clk, reset, count[3:0]; reg [3:0] count declared inside
always @(posedge clk or posedge reset) with non-blocking assignment count <= count + 1
Test bench with no ports, reg for clock and reset, wire for count, DUT instantiated by name
Clock generation by always #5 clk = ~clk; reset pulse then repeated clock edges
Correct use of non-blocking assignment in sequential logic
Compile and elaborate with a simulator, run, inspect waveforms or $monitor output

bank.q: Write Verilog for a 1-bit full adder in gate level and in dataflow style, and write a test bench that applies all input combinations and checks the outputs.
outline: Gate level: two xor, two and, one or primitive instances with named wires
Dataflow: assign sum = a ^ b ^ cin; assign cout = (a & b) | (b & cin) | (a & cin);
Test bench: regs a, b, cin; wires sum, cout; instantiate both versions
Stimulus: exhaustive loop or #10 steps through 8 input combinations
$monitor or $display and, if possible, a self-check against expected values
Observation: both descriptions must match at every step

bank.q: A netlist of 100,000 standard cells is ready. Explain what floorplanning, placement and routing do to it, in order, and what is checked after each.
outline: Floorplan: die size and aspect ratio, macro and memory positions, I/O pin assignment, power plan, placement blockages
Checks: area utilisation, pin accessibility, power-grid IR drop estimate
Placement: global then detailed, rows of standard cells, objectives of wire length and congestion, timing-driven placement
Checks: congestion map, estimated timing, cell density, no overlaps
Clock-tree synthesis between placement and routing
Routing: global routing assigns tracks, detailed routing draws wires and vias; DRC, timing and crosstalk checks after routing

bank.q: You must add a soft-core processor to an FPGA system-on-chip. Explain the steps: bus connection, memory map, wrapper and clock-domain crossing.
outline: Select a soft-core and its bus interface (e.g. a standard on-chip bus)
Assign address ranges to program memory, data memory and peripherals; document the memory map
Wrap the processor core and each peripheral with a wrapper that adapts signals and bus protocol
Reset and interrupt wiring, boot memory contents
Clock-domain crossing: processor clock versus peripheral clock; use async FIFOs or synchronisers
Verify with a test bench that runs a small program through the memory map

bank.q: A startup in Chennai must ship 5,000 units of a signal-processing board in six months. Compare an ASIC and an FPGA implementation on NRE, unit cost, performance, power and time to market, and recommend one.
outline: ASIC: high fixed NRE (masks, EDA, IP, packaging), low unit cost at volume, best speed and power
FPGA: near-zero NRE, higher unit cost, lower clock speed, more power, but reprogrammable in the field
Break-even volume analysis: fixed cost divided by per-unit saving
Schedule: ASIC adds physical design, signoff and fabrication months; FPGA can be re-programmed after a bug
Risk: respin cost of an ASIC versus bitstream update of an FPGA
Justified recommendation for 5,000 units and six months

bank.q: Discuss test cost metrics and test economics. Analyse the trade-off between external ATE testing, scan-based ATPG and BIST for a large logic chip.
outline: Cost drivers: tester time per device, pattern count, tester pin count and capital cost, yield learning
Test time equals pattern count times shift and capture cycles; more coverage usually means more patterns
ATE with scan ATPG: high coverage, needs a tester, more pins and memory for patterns
BIST: on-chip generation, runs at speed, but area overhead and limited diagnosis
Fault coverage versus cost curve; escape cost and customer returns
Balanced scheme: BIST for memories and embedded blocks, scan ATPG for random logic

bank.q: Compare full-custom and semi-custom design styles. When is each justified, and how does the choice change the design flow?
outline: Full-custom: every transistor drawn by hand, best area, speed and power, longest schedule and highest effort
Semi-custom: standard cells or gate/field-programmable arrays, library-based synthesis and place-and-route
Flow differences: full-custom needs schematic entry, layout editing, extraction and intensive DRC/LVS iteration
Semi-custom relies on characterised libraries, timing-driven synthesis and signoff with standard reports
Suitable cases: full-custom for high-volume processors, memories and analog; semi-custom for most digital logic
Cost, risk and reuse argument in the conclusion

bank.q: Analyse how floorplanning decisions propagate through placement and routing. Show what fails at signoff when a floorplan is poor.
outline: Macro positions and aspect ratio fix the distance between communicating blocks and the routing channels
Pin assignment sets where signals enter; wrong side forces long detours
Utilisation too high leaves no space for the router: congestion and detours
Congestion raises wire length, which raises delay, dynamic power and crosstalk
Clock-tree and power-grid need space in the floorplan; ignoring them causes IR drop and skew failures
Feedback loop: congestion or timing violations force re-floorplanning; automated tools iterate, designers set constraints

glossary.def: A chip manufactured for one fixed function, customised through masks at fabrication.
Register-transfer level: a description of sequential logic as registers and the combinational logic between them.
A list of cells and the nets that connect their pins, the usual output of synthesis.
A Verilog module, with no ports, that generates stimulus and checks the outputs of a design instance.
Design Under Test: the instantiated module that a test bench exercises.
Design for testability: on-chip structures added to make internal nodes controllable and observable from the pins.
Automatic test pattern generation: software that computes input patterns to detect modelled faults.
Built-in self-test: on-chip circuitry that generates test patterns and compresses the responses.
A series of scan flip-flops linked into a shift register so test data can be loaded and unloaded serially.
An abstract representation of a physical defect, such as a line stuck-at 0, used for test generation.
The final set of checks (timing, power, physical verification) that must pass before tapeout.
A style where the designer draws and optimises every transistor and its layout by hand.
A style that uses pre-characterised cells or a pre-built array and customises mainly the interconnection.
Lookup table: a small memory in an FPGA that holds the truth table of a combinational function.
Configurable logic block: an FPGA tile holding lookup tables, flip-flops and carry logic.
Field-programmable gate array: a chip whose logic cells and wiring are configured by a bitstream after manufacture.
Complex programmable logic device: a small programmable part with macrocells and a central switch matrix.
A pre-designed, verified functional block that is licensed and reused in a larger chip.
IP delivered as synthesizable HDL source, mapped to the user's technology at build time.
IP delivered as a fixed physical layout for one process, with guaranteed timing and area.
A processor supplied as HDL and implemented in the programmable or standard-cell fabric.
Logic placed around a reused block to adapt its signal names, bus protocol, clocks and resets to the surrounding system.
A connection between logic on two unrelated clocks, needing synchronisers or asynchronous FIFOs.
Assigning die area, macro positions, pin locations and power structure before placement.
Choosing the exact die coordinate of each cell with the aim of short wires and low congestion.
Creating the metal wires and vias that realise the nets between placed cells.
